byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: 331 million people counted, nine in ten online, and an unemployment rate that touched 14.7 percent in April.

items.title: Population
items.summary: The 2020 census counted 331.4 million people, 93.8 to the square mile.

sources.label: U.S. Census Bureau: Decennial census historical facts, 2020

items.title: Life expectancy at birth
items.summary: Life expectancy at birth fell to about 77 years in 2020, from 78.5 in 2010.

items.title: Out of work
items.summary: Unemployment reached 14.7 percent in April 2020, when 20.5 million nonfarm jobs were lost, as reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics on 8 May.

items.title: The economy shrank
items.summary: Real GDP contracted 3.5 percent in 2020, the biggest contraction since 1946.

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: Face masks became part of the outfit, and comfort beat formality at home.

items.title: The mask as accessory
items.summary: At the start of the pandemic wearing a face mask became common and often mandatory; shortages and easy home-made designs led to many styles, and people matched masks to their outfits.

items.title: Comfort at home
items.summary: Lockdowns led a generation of women to prefer comfortable clothes at home, and 'comfortcore' trends followed from 2020 to 2022.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 2020s in fashion

items.title: Pajamas for class
items.summary: K-12 and university students favoured pajamas, sweatpants and athleisure during remote learning.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 2020s in fashion

items.title: Cottagecore
items.summary: Taylor Swift's 2020 albums Folklore and Evermore reinforced the cottagecore trend.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 2020s in fashion

items.title: Clothes shops empty
items.summary: Clothing sales fell 89 percent in the two months to April 2020, and retail sales overall fell 8.3 percent in March and 16.4 percent in April.

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: Millions lost their jobs in weeks, and many who kept them worked from home.

items.title: Claims by the million
items.summary: On 19 March 281,000 Americans filed for unemployment, then 3.28 million on 26 March, the largest weekly increase in U.S. history; weekly claims peaked at 6.9 million on 28 March.

sources.label: Wikipedia: COVID-19 pandemic in the United States
Wikipedia: Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States

items.title: The CARES Act
items.summary: The CARES Act, signed on 27 March 2020, raised unemployment benefits by $600 a week, in a relief package of roughly $2 trillion.

sources.label: Wikipedia: COVID-19 pandemic in the United States
Wikipedia: Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States

items.title: Stay at home
items.summary: On 20 March New York ordered staff at non-essential businesses to stay home, and by 31 March about three-quarters of the U.S. population was under lockdown restrictions.

sources.label: Wikipedia: COVID-19 pandemic in the United States

items.title: A pause on evictions
items.summary: The CARES Act gave a 120-day eviction moratorium for federally backed properties from 27 March to 24 July 2020, covering about 28 percent of rental units; a CDC nationwide moratorium ran from 1 September to the end of 2020.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States

schoolAndChildhood.title: Growing up
schoolAndChildhood.standfirst: Most schools closed in mid-March, and classes moved to video calls.

items.title: Schools close
items.summary: Most schools nationwide were closed by 16 March 2020.

sources.label: Wikipedia: COVID-19 pandemic in the United States

items.title: Zoom in class
items.summary: Zoom use for distance education surged; New York City's Department of Education banned Zoom over security and privacy concerns and lifted the ban in May 2020 after the company addressed them.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Zoom (software)

items.title: The Canadian border
items.summary: On 18 March 2020 the United States temporarily closed its border with Canada to non-trade travel.

keepingInTouch.title: Keeping in touch
keepingInTouch.standfirst: Video calls replaced the office, the classroom and the family gathering.

items.title: Ten million to two hundred million
items.summary: Zoom had a maximum of 10 million daily meeting participants in December 2019 and more than 200 million in March 2020.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Zoom (software)

items.title: A claim walked back
items.summary: Zoom's April 2020 claim of 300 million daily meeting participants was later retracted, since the metric counts joins, which can happen several times a day.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Zoom (software)

items.title: The 40-minute limit
items.summary: Zoom's free plan allowed up to 100 participants with a 40-minute limit per meeting, and in April 2020 the company raised its default security settings against 'Zoombombing'.

healthAndMedicine.title: Health and medicine
healthAndMedicine.standfirst: By year's end more than 300,000 people had died, and the first vaccines were authorised.

items.title: The first deaths
items.summary: The first U.S. death from COVID-19 was reported in Washington state on 29 February 2020; deaths passed 1,000 on 25 March and 10,000 on 6 April.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 2020 in the United States

items.title: Cloth face coverings
items.summary: On 3 April 2020 the CDC recommended cloth face coverings in public.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 2020 in the United States

items.title: Deaths through the year
items.summary: U.S. deaths from COVID-19 passed 100,000 by 27 May, 200,000 on 22 September and 300,000 on 14 December 2020; vaccines became available under emergency use in December.

sources.label: Wikipedia: COVID-19 pandemic in the United States

leisureAndFun.title: Evenings, weekends and festivals
leisureAndFun.standfirst: In March the cinemas, theatres and stadiums emptied, and by 24 March the national box office was zero.

items.title: The lights go out
items.summary: SXSW was cancelled for the first time in 34 years on 6 March, the NBA suspended its season on 11 March, and the NCAA cancelled its March tournaments and Broadway theatres closed on 12 March 2020.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 2020 in the United States

items.title: Zero at the box office
items.summary: U.S. box office revenue was zero on 24 March 2020, a first.

items.title: Super Bowl LIV
items.summary: The Kansas City Chiefs beat the San Francisco 49ers 31-20 in Super Bowl LIV on 2 February 2020.

sources.label: Wikipedia: 2020 in the United States

items.title: The Derby moves
items.summary: The Kentucky Derby was postponed from May to 5 September on 16 March 2020.

spotlight.title: Lockdown life
spotlight.standfirst: In March 2020 an emergency was declared, schools and offices closed, and within weeks about three in four Americans were under stay-at-home restrictions.

items.title: The first case
items.summary: The CDC confirmed the first U.S. case on 21 January 2020 (another page dates it to 20 January); the Health Secretary declared a public health emergency on 31 January.

items.summary: On 13 March 2020 the president declared a national emergency and freed $50 billion in disaster relief funds.
